title: Infants around four months looked longer when a wide object hid behind a too-narrow screen
summary: Wang, Baillargeon, and Brueckner reported that infants around four months looked longer when a wide object ended fully hidden behind a screen too narrow to hide it.
body: In a 2004 paper in Cognition, Wang, Baillargeon, and Brueckner tested infants around four months with test trials only, and no habituation first. In the first experiment, 32 infants saw a wide object lowered behind a wide screen or a narrow screen. The experimental infants looked longer at the narrow-screen outcome. Control infants, shown a narrow object that could fit behind either screen, looked about equally. The authors read the longer look as heightened attention when an expectation about the hidden object was violated. The result is that experiment, not a statement about every infant.

sources.title: Young infants' reasoning about hidden objects: evidence from violation-of-expectation tasks with test trials only
sources.author: Su-hua Wang, Renée Baillargeon, and Laura Brueckner
sources.note: Supports Experiment 1 as the paper reports it: longer looking at the narrow-occluder event, about-equal looking in the narrow-object control, test trials only. Cognition 2004;93(3):167-198.
